title: Alma addresses his son’s concern
summary: Alma identifies his son’s concern about the justice of punishing sinners. He begins to explain by recounting the first parents’ departure from Eden and the guarding of the tree of life.

explicit_facts.text: Alma says his son is troubled by the justice of God in the punishment of the sinner.
Alma says he will explain and recounts that the Lord God sent the first parents from Eden to till the ground.
Alma recounts that the Lord God placed cherubim and a flaming sword at the east end of Eden to guard the tree of life.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Alma speaks to his son, who may be shown listening.
unspecified_visual_details: The son’s name, appearance, and age.
The physical setting of the conversation.

spoken_dialogue.text: my son, I perceive there is somewhat more which doth worry your mind
spoken_dialogue.speaker: Alma (son of Alma)

spoken_dialogue.text: my son, I will explain this thing unto thee.
spoken_dialogue.speaker: Alma (son of Alma)

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The Eden account is part of Alma’s explanation, not a simultaneous event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not name the son.
Do not depict the Eden account as occurring during this conversation.
Do not invent an appearance for the Lord God.

title: Alma explains the guarded tree of life
summary: Alma tells his son he will explain. He recounts that the Lord God sent our first parents from the garden of Eden to till the ground, drew out the man, and placed cherubim and a turning flaming sword at the garden’s east end to keep the tree of life.
characters: Alma’s son (unnamed in the supplied verses)

explicit_facts.text: Alma addresses his son and says he will explain.
The Lord God sent our first parents forth from the garden of Eden to till the ground and drew out the man.
The Lord God placed cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way at the garden’s east end to keep the tree of life.
The man had become as God, knowing good and evil; the cherubim and sword were placed so that he would not partake of the fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Alma and his son may be shown during Alma’s explanation, without depicting the recounted Eden events as happening then.
unspecified_visual_details: The conversation’s location and the appearances of Alma and his son are not specified.
The appearances of the Lord God and cherubim are not specified.

spoken_dialogue.text: Now behold, my son, I will explain this thing unto thee.
spoken_dialogue.speaker: Alma the Younger

spoken_dialogue.text: For behold, after the Lord God sent our first parents forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground, from whence they were taken—
spoken_dialogue.speaker: Alma the Younger

spoken_dialogue.text: Now, we see that the man had become as God, knowing good and evil;
spoken_dialogue.speaker: Alma the Younger

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The Eden events are recounted, not described as occurring during Alma’s explanation.
Taking and eating the fruit is presented as a possibility the guards were placed to prevent, not as an event that occurred.
prohibited_inventions: Do not stage the recounted Eden events as occurring during Alma’s explanation.
Do not invent an appearance for the Lord God or cherubim.
Do not depict the man taking or eating the fruit.
Do not give Alma’s son a name based on material outside the supplied verses.

title: A probationary time
summary: Alma explains that preventing access to the tree of life allowed a time for mankind to repent and serve God.

explicit_facts.text: The man had become as God, knowing good and evil, and was prevented from taking and eating from the tree of life.
A time was granted to mankind to repent and serve God.
Alma says that if Adam had immediately eaten from the tree of life, he would have lived forever without space for repentance, frustrating the plan of salvation.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Use a symbolic treatment of time granted for repentance rather than inventing a specific event.
unspecified_visual_details: Any visible people, location, or visual representation of the probationary period.

narration.text: there was a time granted unto man to repent
a probationary time, a time to repent and serve God.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The hypothetical immediate eating in verse 5 is not narrated as an event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict Adam eating the fruit or portray the hypothetical outcome as something that happened.

title: Mortality and the Fall
summary: Alma teaches that mankind was appointed to die and that the first parents were cut off temporally and spiritually from the Lord’s presence.

explicit_facts.text: Mankind was appointed to die and was cut off from the tree of life and the face of the earth; Alma describes them as fallen.
The first parents were cut off temporally and spiritually from the Lord’s presence.
Alma says reclaiming man from temporal death was not expedient because it would destroy the plan of happiness.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Represent separation from the Lord’s presence symbolically, without inventing a visible divine appearance.
unspecified_visual_details: Any physical depiction of death, separation, or the plan of happiness.

narration.text: our first parents were cut off both temporally and spiritually

doctrinal_or_story_notes: These verses explain doctrine rather than narrate a new event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict a death or a divine figure as visibly present.

title: Spiritual death and preparation
summary: Alma teaches that mankind’s probationary state became a preparation for reclaiming them from spiritual death, and describes the consequence without redemption.

explicit_facts.text: The Fall brought spiritual and temporal death, and mankind needed reclaiming from spiritual death.
The probationary state became a preparatory state.
Without the plan of redemption, souls would be miserable after death, cut off from the Lord’s presence.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Use abstract or symbolic imagery for preparation and separation; no particular visual event is required.
unspecified_visual_details: How the preparatory state or spiritual death appears visually.

narration.text: this probationary state became a state for them to prepare
it became a preparatory state.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Verse 11 states a consequence in a counterfactual condition, not a depicted death scene.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict souls visibly suffering or invent an afterlife location.

title: Justice and the conditions of redemption
summary: Alma teaches that redemption depends on repentance in the preparatory state and that justice holds fallen mankind accountable.

explicit_facts.text: There was no means to reclaim mankind from the fallen state brought about by disobedience.
The plan of redemption could be brought about only on conditions of repentance; justice could not be destroyed.
All mankind were fallen and subject to God’s justice, cut off from his presence.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A symbolic balance or other abstract image may suggest justice, but is not specified.
unspecified_visual_details: Any visual personification or physical form of justice and redemption.

narration.text: the plan of redemption could not be brought about, only on conditions of repentance

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The passage is instruction, not a narrated event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict personified Justice, a courtroom, or a specific act of punishment as occurring.

title: The plan of mercy and atonement
summary: Alma teaches that an atonement makes the plan of mercy possible and that punishment stands opposite the plan of happiness.

explicit_facts.text: The plan of mercy required an atonement; God himself atones for the sins of the world, appeasing justice and bringing mercy.
Repentance requires punishment, which is eternal as the soul’s life, set opposite the plan of happiness.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The atonement and the plans may be conveyed through restrained symbolic imagery.
unspecified_visual_details: The visual form of the atonement, mercy, justice, or the plan of happiness.

narration.text: God himself atoneth for the sins of the world
to bring about the plan of mercy

doctrinal_or_story_notes: No atonement event is described in this chapter; these are doctrinal statements.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict a specific atonement event or show God’s appearance.

title: Law, sin, and punishment
summary: The passage asks how repentance, sin, law, and punishment relate. It states that a just law and an affixed punishment brought remorse of conscience, poses a hypothetical question about fear of death for murder, and states that without law against sin, men would not fear sinning.

explicit_facts.text: The passage asks how a man could repent without sin, sin without law, or have law without punishment.
A punishment was affixed and a just law given, bringing remorse of conscience unto man.
The passage asks whether a man would fear death for murder if no law specified that consequence.
Without a law against sin, men would not be afraid to sin.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The hypothetical and questions can be presented as text rather than enacted.
unspecified_visual_details: Any background or visual design accompanying the text.

narration.text: Now, how could a man repent except he should sin?
Now, there was a punishment affixed, and a just law given, which brought remorse of conscience unto man.
would he be afraid he would die if he should murder?
men would not be afraid to sin.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The murder example is a hypothetical question, not a narrated event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict a murder, victim, punishment being carried out, or an appearance or setting not supplied by these verses.
Do not assign these words to a named or visibly depicted speaker.

title: Justice, mercy, and repentance
summary: The passage asks what justice or mercy could claim without law. It teaches that law, punishment, and repentance are given; mercy claims the penitent because of the atonement, which brings resurrection and restoration to God's presence for judgment.

explicit_facts.text: The passage asks what justice or mercy could do if no law were given.
A law, a punishment, and repentance are given.
Mercy claims the penitent and comes because of the atonement.
The atonement brings about resurrection; people are restored to God's presence to be judged according to their works, the law, and justice.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Present the teaching through text rather than staging its doctrinal events.
unspecified_visual_details: The physical setting and appearance of any speaker or listener.
The appearance of resurrection, judgment, or God's presence.

narration.text: But there is a law given, and a punishment affixed, and a repentance granted;
mercy claimeth the penitent,
and mercy cometh because of the atonement;
and the atonement bringeth to pass the resurrection of the dead;

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Resurrection and judgment are taught here, not narrated as events occurring in the scene.
The supplied verses do not identify a speaker.
prohibited_inventions: Do not assign the words to a named speaker or invent dialogue.
Do not stage a resurrection or judgment, or invent God's appearance.

title: Mercy does not rob justice
summary: Alma states that justice and mercy each claim what is theirs, only the truly penitent are saved, and God’s purposes bring salvation and redemption as well as destruction and misery.

explicit_facts.text: Justice exercises its demands and mercy claims what is its own; only the truly penitent are saved.
Mercy cannot rob justice; otherwise God would cease to be God.
God brings about his eternal purposes, including salvation and redemption, and destruction and misery.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A symbolic contrast may accompany Alma’s teaching, without depicting abstractions as literal beings.
unspecified_visual_details: Visual representations of mercy, justice, salvation, or destruction.

narration.text: none but the truly penitent are saved.
mercy can rob justice?

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Mercy and justice are figures of speech and should not be portrayed as visible people.
prohibited_inventions: Do not literalize mercy or justice as characters.

title: An invitation and restoration
summary: Alma teaches that anyone willing may come and partake of the waters of life freely, and that a person’s deeds will be restored to them.

explicit_facts.text: Whoever will come may freely partake of the waters of life; whoever will not come is not compelled, and in the last day each is restored according to deeds.
Evil will be done to a person who desired evil and did not repent, according to God’s restoration.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Treat “waters of life” as a figure of speech, not a literal miraculous scene.
unspecified_visual_details: The visual form of the waters of life and the last-day restoration.

narration.text: whosoever will come may come and partake of the waters of life freely

doctrinal_or_story_notes: These verses are instruction and conditional teaching, not a narrated event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict literal supernatural waters or an enacted last-day judgment.

title: Alma urges his son to repent
summary: Alma urges his son to let his concern trouble him no more, to allow his sins to bring him to repentance, and to let God’s justice, mercy, and long-suffering have full sway in his heart.

explicit_facts.text: Alma asks his son to let these matters trouble him no more and to let his sins trouble him toward repentance.
Alma tells his son not to deny God’s justice or excuse his sins, but to let justice, mercy, and long-suffering have full sway in his heart and bring him to humility.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Alma may be shown speaking to his son in the same unspecified teaching setting.
unspecified_visual_details: The son’s identity, appearance, and the setting.

narration.text: let your sins trouble you, with that trouble which shall bring you down unto repentance.

prohibited_inventions: Do not identify or name Alma’s son.

title: Alma commissions his son to preach
summary: Alma tells his son that God has called him to preach and sends him to declare the word truthfully and soberly, praying that God will grant according to his words.

explicit_facts.text: Alma says his son is called of God to preach the word to the people.
Alma tells his son to go and declare the word with truth and soberness to bring souls to repentance.
Alma prays that God will grant his son according to his words and concludes, “Amen.”

reasonable_visual_inferences: Alma may be shown concluding his instruction to his son; no departure is specified.
unspecified_visual_details: Whether the son departs, the setting, and either person’s appearance.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The command to go is not evidence that the son visibly departs in this moment.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show a journey or subsequent preaching event.
